posts.title: Walking lunches are back for the autumn
posts.excerpt: With cooler air settling over Hollin Moor, our brown paper walking lunches have returned for guests spending their days on the fell trails.
posts.content:
As November arrives in Cumbria, the morning mist hangs low over the drystone walls along Fell Lane. The first frost has settled across the kitchen garden beds that Kofi Mensah-Lyle tends behind the barn, and the fells above Hollin Moor have turned a deep bronze. With the colder winds coming off the high ridges, we have brought back our packed walking lunches for guests heading out for the day. For £14 per person, each lunch is prepared after breakfast and wrapped in greaseproof paper and plain brown twine, ready to be dropped into a rucksack beside walking boots in the front hall.

The foundation of each parcel begins early in the morning. At 06:40, Ines Calloway opens the dining room shutters to let in the dawn light and puts the kettle on, while Maren Holt shapes the morning dough at the floured kitchen table. The sourdough loaves come out of the oven in time for breakfast at 07:30, and the same fresh bread is sliced thick for the trail. Slices are layered with roasted root vegetables and winter greens harvested by Kofi, farmhouse cheeses from neighboring valleys, and homemade pickles prepared in Rafael Oduya's kitchen. Alongside the sandwich, each parcel holds an apple from the lane, a wedge of dark fruit cake, and a flask of hot vegetable broth or tea.

Walks from the door set out around 09:30. On Tuesdays and Thursdays, Arthur Penhale waits on the bench outside to guide guests along the high routes, while on other days guests take map cards from the reading room table. Some choose the sheltered larch path, a 4 km route taking 1½ hours beneath trees that are now shedding golden needles into the damp grass. Others take the 7 km trail up to Hollin Tarn, taking 2½ hours to reach the cold slate rocks above the water, sitting to unwrap their bread while the wind sweeps across the open fell. For those attempting the 14 km Ridge of the Moor, the 5-hour trek requires steady footing, making a warm broth at midday essential.

There is a particular satisfaction in eating a simple meal on the open fell when the sky is pale grey and the valley below seems vast and silent. At 12:30, when guests unwrap their packages on a hillside or beside a stone shelter, the house remains quiet back in Hollin Moor. By mid-afternoon, boots return to the stone porch, muddy and wet from the moorland turf. Guests slip off their boots and head straight into the warm reading room, where Yuna Park serves hot tea and fresh biscuits at 15:30.

Shortly after three, Kofi lights the birch wood stove in the timber bath house out on the courtyard deck. By 16:00, steam rises against the darkening fells, and the bath house remains warm until 21:30. Soaking in hot water while looking out at the mountain twilight is the natural conclusion to hours spent on the ridge. At 19:00, everyone gathers at the long dining table for Rafael's four-course dinner, where stories of the day's trails are shared over warm bowls and flickering candlelight. By 22:00, the farmhouse grows quiet, ready for another day on Hollin Moor.

posts.title: Larches turning on the Hollin path
posts.excerpt: The larch needles above the tarn have turned their pale autumn gold, marking the quietest weeks of the walking season before the November mists settle.
posts.content:
The larch needles above the tarn have turned their pale autumn gold, marking the quietest weeks of the walking season before the November mists settle.

The path starts at the garden gate and takes about an hour and a half out and back. It is four kilometres, mostly level, and best before eleven when the light comes through the trees.

Come back for the bath house, which is warm from four o’clock.

posts.title: Bread at six
posts.excerpt: Maren is in the kitchen before six every morning; by half past seven the first loaf is on the table.
posts.content:
Maren is in the kitchen before six every morning. The dough is mixed the evening before and shaped by lamp light.

By half past seven the first loaf is on the breakfast table with butter and eggs from the lane.

If you wake early, the kitchen door is open and there is usually tea.

posts.title: Quiet Weeks for March are open
posts.excerpt: A Quiet Week is seven nights, Sunday to Sunday, in any room, with 15% off the nightly rate.
posts.content:
A Quiet Week is seven nights, Sunday to Sunday, in any room, with 15% off. It starts from £1,250.

Breakfast and dinner are included, and there is no programme: the day is paced by the house.

Write to us or check the dates on the Rates & Booking page.
